title: Rearrange Without Neighbours
statement:
Can the letters of `letters` be put in a different order so that **no two equal letters are next to each other**? Every letter must be used exactly once.

Return `true` if such an order exists, otherwise `false`.
constraints: letters uses only lowercase English letters

examples.explanation: Three `a`s need at least two other letters between them, but there is only one `b`.

hints.nudge: At each position, which letter is the most dangerous to leave for later? Which letter should you place so the problem does not get stuck?
hints.pattern: Greedy with a max-heap of letter counts: always place the most frequent remaining letter that is not the one you just placed.
hints.pseudocode:
heap = (count, letter) for each letter, largest count first
held = nothing
while heap or held:
  if heap is empty: return false
  take the top (count, letter); place it
  if held: push held back; held = nothing
  if count > 1: held = (count - 1, letter)
return true
hints.walkthrough: Trying every order is n! work. Greedy works: the letter with the most copies left is the hardest to place, so use it whenever you can. Because the same letter cannot be placed twice in a row, after placing a letter set it aside for one round (`held`) and put it back into the heap after the NEXT letter has been placed. If the heap is empty while a letter is still held, the only letter left would have to go next to itself: return false. When everything has been placed, return true. A faster check without the heap: it is possible exactly when the most frequent letter appears at most (n + 1) / 2 times.
